slide_text: Inventing RAG and Agentic AI Every concept in this curriculum is something you will build before it is named. You will hit a wall, feel the frustration of a broken approach, and then invent the fix yourself. Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

Challenge (skip ahead if you can): An LLM can't answer questions about a private knowledge base, and a single search isn't enough for multi-hop questions. Build a tiny agent that does retrieval-augmented answering in a loop: search the docs, decide whether it has enough, and if not, search again with a refined query. Then answer from the retrieved text only. [code block] [code block] Already got it? The next slides will guide you step by step.

Part 1: The Knowledge Gap The central question: what does an LLM actually know, and what happens when it doesn't? Prerequisites. Basic Python (functions, lists, dicts, loops). No ML background required. Companion files — download these alongside the curriculum: — all datasets used across every exercise. Import what you need. — step-by-step instructions for setting up Anthropic or OpenAI.

The Amnesiac Oracle Install the Anthropic SDK and run the observe code below. Both answers come back instantly and correctly. Now ask the model something it cannot possibly know — an internal company document it has never seen. Read the answer carefully. Your task: The model answered confidently. Is that answer trustworthy? How would you know? Write a new version of called . Before calling the API, check whether the question contains the phrase or . If it does, return a plain string: Otherwise, call the API normally. This keyword check is brittle. In one sentence, describe why it will fail for most real questions. Hint 1 For step 2, think about using an statement that checks or . Return the fallback string early if either matches. Hint 2 For step 3, imagine someone asks about last quarter's revenue without using the exact words "internal memo" or "Q3 2024." Your check would miss it completely.

You have just felt the core problem: a language model's knowledge is frozen at training time. It cannot know what happened yesterday, or what is in your company's private database. Your keyword check is a crude patch. The real fix requires giving the model the document at the moment it is asked. What you invented: the intuition behind retrieval-augmented generation — the idea that knowledge should come from outside the model, not from inside it.

Stuffing the Prompt Import the Acme Corp policy documents and try putting all three directly into the prompt (see the observe code). It works — the model answers correctly from the documents. The problem. Imagine you have 10,000 documents instead of 3, each 500 words. Run the calculation code below. You cannot stuff all 10,000 into the prompt. Your task. Write a function that uses simple keyword matching to pick the most relevant document: Split the question into individual words (lowercase). For each document, count how many of those words appear in the document text (lowercase). Return only the single document with the highest count. Test it with at least two different questions. Does it always pick the right document? Hint 1 Use to get individual words. Then for each doc, count how many of those words appear in . Hint 2 Use Python's built-in with a argument: .

You have just reinvented keyword-based retrieval. It is fast and requires no ML. But try this question: — the word "hotel" does not appear, and "accommodation" might not match "lodging." You would miss documents that mean the same thing but use different words. What you invented: the idea of retrieval as a first step — only sending relevant context to the model. This is the skeleton of RAG. The next part fixes the keyword-matching weakness.

Quick Check 1.1 — Why Keyword Matching Fails Your function uses keyword matching. A user asks: "What is the per-night accommodation limit?" but the relevant document says "hotel expenses are capped at $200 per night." Why does your function fail? A. The function is too slow to process the question B. The words "accommodation" and "hotel" mean the same thing but share no letters, so the keyword count is zero C. The function only works with questions shorter than 10 words D. Python's does not work on questions with punctuation Answer: B. Keyword matching compares exact words. "Accommodation" and "hotel" are different words that happen to mean similar things. This is exactly the problem that embeddings (Part 2) will solve.
Part 2: The Search Problem The central question: how do you find a document that means the same thing, even when it uses different words?

When Words Lie Build a tiny keyword search engine using the mini corpus (see the observe code). The first sentence scores highest because it shares the word "hotel." But the second and third sentences mean exactly the same thing and score zero — they share no words with the query. Your task. Measure meaning using numbers instead of words. Install and run the provided code. Each sentence becomes a vector of 384 numbers. Implement dot-product similarity between two vectors: sum of for all . Write it with a loop (no numpy). Build a function that embeds the query, computes dot products against all corpus embeddings, and returns results sorted by score. Do the accommodation and lodging sentences now rank above the Python sentence? Hint 1 For the dot product, loop over both vectors at the same time: . Hint 2 For , embed the query once, then compute the dot product with every corpus embedding. Use a list of pairs and sort by score descending.

You have just used embeddings — lists of numbers that capture what words and sentences mean. The dot product between two embedding vectors tells you how similar the meaning of two pieces of text is. This is the engine inside every modern search system. What you invented: semantic search using vector embeddings — the retrieval backbone of production RAG systems.

Building a Document Index In the real world, you embed documents once (when they are added to the system) and store those embeddings. At query time, you only embed the question — not all the documents again. Your task. Build a simple in-memory vector store. Step 1 — Write an function that takes the list of structured documents and returns a list of pairs. Step 2 — Write a function that embeds the query, computes dot product with every indexed embedding, and returns the top-k most relevant documents. Step 3 — If you had 1 million documents, computing a dot product with each one would be slow. In one or two sentences, describe what you might do to speed this up. Hint 1 For , loop through each doc, embed its text, and append a tuple to a list. Hint 2 For , reuse your dot-product function from the previous exercise. Sort the results and slice with . Hint 3 For Step 3: think about grouping similar documents together so you only compare the query against a small cluster, not all one million. This is the idea behind approximate nearest-neighbor search.

What you invented: a vector index — the data structure at the heart of systems like Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector. You embed documents once, store the vectors, and at query time only embed the question.

Quick Check 2.1 — Embeddings and Dot Products You embed the query "hotel policy" and two documents. Document A (about hotel rules) has a dot product of 0.87 with the query. Document B (about Python loops) has a dot product of 0.12. Which document is more relevant, and why? A. Document B, because lower scores mean better matches B. Document A, because a higher dot product means the meanings are more similar C. Neither — dot products only work with numbers, not text D. You cannot tell without knowing the exact embedding vectors Answer: B. A higher dot product between two embedding vectors means the texts are more similar in meaning. Document A (about hotel rules) is clearly more relevant to a hotel policy query.
Part 3: Inventing RAG The central question: how do you combine retrieval with generation to get answers that are grounded in your documents?

The Grounded Answer You now have two working pieces: a retrieval system and a language model. Try connecting them naively (see the observe code). It works — but there is a subtle problem. The problem. Ask a question completely outside the documents: Does the model say "I don't know" or does it answer from general knowledge? Your task. Improve into with two changes: Improve the prompt. Add a clear instruction: "Answer only using the context provided. If the context does not contain the answer, respond with exactly: I cannot answer this from the provided documents." Add a confidence gate: after retrieval, check the top similarity score. If the best-matching document scores below , skip the API call entirely and return the fallback string directly. Hint 1 For the prompt improvement, add a system message or prepend instructions like: "You are a helpful assistant. Only answer using the context below. If the context does not contain the answer, say so." Hint 2 For the confidence gate, your function should also return the similarity score. Check before calling the API.

You have just built a complete RAG pipeline: retrieve relevant chunks, gate on confidence, generate a grounded answer. The confidence gate is a simple but important production pattern — it prevents the model from hallucinating when retrieval fails. What you invented: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — the dominant architecture for grounding LLMs in private or recent knowledge.

Chunking and the Goldilocks Problem Real documents are long. If you embed an entire 10-page PDF as one vector, you lose precision — the embedding averages out over too many topics. But if you split every sentence into its own chunk, each chunk loses context. There is a Goldilocks size. Your task. Write a function that splits a document into overlapping chunks of approximately words, with words repeated at the start of each new chunk. Then index the chunks and test retrieval with the provided questions. Finally, experiment : change to 20 (very small) and then to 200 (very large). How does retrieval quality change? Hint 1 Split the text into a list of words first: . Then use a loop that steps by each time. Hint 2 Each chunk is . Advance by so that words repeat at the beginning of the next chunk.
What you invented: document chunking with overlap — a standard preparation step in all production RAG systems. The overlap prevents relevant sentences from being split across chunk boundaries.

Quick Check 3.1 — The RAG Pipeline In your RAG pipeline, the confidence gate checks whether the best-matching document's similarity score is above 0.35. What happens when a user asks "What is the speed of light?" and none of your company documents are about physics? A. The model answers correctly from its training data B. The model hallucinates a wrong answer using the closest document C. The confidence gate blocks the question because all similarity scores are below 0.35, and returns the fallback message D. The system crashes because no document matches Answer: C. The confidence gate catches this case. Since no document is relevant (all scores below 0.35), it returns the fallback string without calling the model at all. This prevents hallucination.
Part 4: The Single-Step Limit The central question: what happens when answering a question requires doing something — not just knowing something?

The Model That Cannot Act Ask the model things that require real-time actions (see the observe code). The time question fails — the model cannot check a clock. The calculator question might work for easy math but could fail on harder ones. The model has no memory between calls and cannot interact with the outside world: it cannot check a clock, run a calculator, search the web, or write a file. Your task. Build a small toolkit of Python functions: , , . Invent a simple protocol. Write a prompt that instructs the model to output tool calls as / , and final answers as . Test it — does the model follow the protocol? Hint 1 For the toolkit, can use and can use (safe for simple math). Hint 2 For the protocol prompt, tell the model: "You have these tools: [list them]. To use a tool, respond with exactly TOOL: name on one line and INPUT: value on the next. When you have the final answer, respond with ANSWER: your response."

The model produces structured text that describes what tool to call. You have to parse that text and actually run the tool. The model is a reasoning engine, not an execution engine. You are the executor. What you invented: the concept of tool use (also called function calling ) — the mechanism that allows language models to request external actions.

Parsing and Executing Tool Calls Complete the loop: parse the model's text output, run the right tool, and feed the result back. Your task. Write a function that: Asks the model a question using the tool prompt. Parses the response using (provided). If it is a tool call, runs the tool using (provided) and prints the result. If it is an answer, returns it. The limitation. Try: — this requires two tool calls ( then ). Your one-step agent can only do one. Hint 1 Use on the model's text output. It returns a tuple like or . Check which one you got. Hint 2 The full flow: call the model, parse the response, if it is a tool call then run the tool with , print the result, and return it. If it is an answer, just return the text.

A single tool call is not enough for complex questions. You need a loop — the model calls a tool, gets a result, decides if it needs another tool, calls again, and so on. That loop is an agent. What you invented: the tool execution loop — the bridge between a model's text output and real-world actions.

Quick Check 4.1 — Tool Use Your model outputs / . Who actually runs the calculation? A. The language model runs it internally and returns the result B. Your Python code parses the model's text output, calls , and feeds the result back to the model C. The API automatically detects math expressions and evaluates them D. The user must manually copy the expression into a calculator Answer: B. The model is a reasoning engine, not an execution engine. It describes what tool to call as text. Your code must parse that text, run the actual tool, and pass the result back.
Part 5: Inventing Agents The central question: how do you give a model the ability to act repeatedly until a task is complete?

The Reasoning Loop An agent is a loop where: The model receives the question and any previous tool results. It decides: do I have enough information to answer, or do I need a tool? If it needs a tool, you run it, add the result to the conversation, and go to step 1. If it has an answer, return it. Your task. Build — a multi-turn agent using a conversation history list. At each step, ask the model, parse the response, and either run a tool (appending the result back to the conversation) or return the final answer. Test with questions requiring different numbers of steps: — 1 step — 1 step — 2 steps — 3 steps Hint 1 Keep a list called (the conversation history). At each step, send the full list to the model and append its reply. Hint 2 When a tool call is detected, run the tool and append the result as a new message (e.g., ). Then loop back and ask the model again with the updated history. Hint 3 Use a loop. Inside, call the model, parse the response. If , return it. If , run the tool and append the result. If you exhaust all steps, return a message saying the agent could not finish.
What you invented: the agentic loop — the core architecture of every AI agent, from simple assistants to autonomous research systems. This is also known as the ReAct pattern (Reasoning + Acting).

Giving the Agent Memory Your agent has no memory between separate calls. Try: first tell it , then ask — the second call fails. Your task. Add a simple external memory store with two new tools: — store a piece of information — retrieve a stored piece of information Update your to include these tools and update to dispatch to them. Then test the two-call sequence above. Hint 1 Use a plain Python dictionary as the memory store: . The tool does and does . Hint 2 In , add two new cases: if the tool name is , parse the key=value string and store it. If , look up the key and return the value.

You have added persistent state to a stateless model. The model itself still forgets between calls — but the system around it remembers. This pattern (external memory + stateless model) is how real production agents are built. What you invented: external agent memory — the pattern used in systems like LangChain's memory modules, AutoGPT's file-based memory, and enterprise AI assistants.

RAG Agent — Combining Everything Your final exercise combines everything: the vector index from Part 2, the grounded generation from Part 3, and the agentic loop from Part 5. Your task. Add a tool that wraps your function. Update the tool prompt to include it. Then build a complete RAG agent that can both retrieve information from documents AND use tools — and decide which it needs at each step. Test with: — retrieval only — retrieval + calculation Store trip details with , then ask about total costs — retrieval + memory + calculation Bonus: Use from acme_datasets to measure your agent's accuracy across 15 question-answer pairs. Hint 1 The tool is just a wrapper: inside it, call your function and return the text of the top results. Hint 2 Add to your tool prompt alongside the existing tools. In , add a case that calls and returns the document text. Hint 3 Your agent loop already works for tools. The only change is that returns document text, which the model can then use to generate a grounded answer on the next iteration.

What you invented: a RAG-powered tool-using agent — an architecture that appears in production systems like Perplexity, enterprise knowledge assistants, and AI copilots. You built it from scratch, from first principles.
What You Invented

Your Inventions vs. Industry Names Exercise What you built Industry name 1.1 Detected unanswerable questions Hallucination detection 1.2 Selected relevant docs before prompting Context injection / prompt stuffing 2.1 Measured meaning with dot products Semantic similarity 2.2 Stored embeddings once, queried many times Vector index 3.1 Retrieved then generated, with a fallback Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) 3.2 Split long docs into overlapping windows Chunking with overlap 4.1 Made the model describe actions as text Tool use / function calling 4.2 Parsed model text and ran the right function Tool dispatcher 5.1 Looped model + tools until task complete Agentic loop / ReAct pattern 5.2 Added persistent storage outside the model External agent memory 5.3 Combined retrieval, tools, memory, and loop RAG agent
Part 7: Reflection Take a moment to think about what you have built, in your own words.

Reflection Answer these questions in your own words — there are no right or wrong answers. In Part 1, you discovered that a language model's knowledge is frozen. Why does stuffing all documents into the prompt not scale? What is the key insight of retrieval? In Part 2, keyword matching failed when words meant the same thing but were spelled differently. How do embeddings solve this? Could you explain embeddings to a friend who has never coded? In Part 3, you added a confidence gate. Why is it important to not call the model when retrieval fails? What could go wrong without the gate? In Part 5, you turned a single-step tool call into a loop . What makes the loop an "agent"? How does the model decide whether to use another tool or give a final answer? You built every piece from scratch. If you had to explain RAG to someone in one sentence, what would you say?

Going Further Once you have completed all exercises, the natural next steps are: Proper vector databases. Replace your in-memory index with ChromaDB or Qdrant — both have free local modes and Python clients. The ReAct paper. Read ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (Yao et al., 2022). It describes the exact loop you built in Exercise 5.1. Anthropic's native tool use. The Anthropic API supports tool/function calling natively — the model returns structured JSON instead of the text protocol you invented. Rewrite your agent using it. Evaluation. Build a tiny evaluation set: 10 questions with known correct answers, and measure how often your agent gets them right. Multi-agent systems. What if one agent specialised in retrieval and another in calculation, and a coordinator decided which to call? That is a multi-agent system — the current frontier.
